paragraphs: The paper studies how to solve a convex optimization problem when a particular local solver is available. Given a point, this solver returns the best solution within a Euclidean ball of radius r around it. The question is how many calls to that local solver are needed to find an approximately optimal solution over a unit ball.

A straightforward approach needs roughly r⁻¹ log(1/ε) calls to reach accuracy ε. The authors develop an accelerated procedure that reduces this to roughly r⁻²ᐟ³ log(1/ε) calls. They also establish a matching lower bound, showing that the improved dependence reaches the limit identified by their oracle analysis.

The paper then connects this abstract solver to implementable methods. For functions whose Hessian is locally stable, it constructs ball solvers using a Newton variant and, in certain cases, stochastic first-order methods. The resulting algorithms improve previous results for logistic and maximum-norm regression, while providing guarantees comparable to leading results for p-norm regression.
neurips-2020-acceleration-with-a-ball-op.tldr: An accelerated convex optimization algorithm uses fewer local ball-minimization calls, with a matching lower bound and applications to regression.

paragraphs: A reward function must communicate both what an agent should accomplish and which unwanted consequences it should avoid. This paper proposes automatically adding a reward that values the ability to complete possible future tasks. Actions that undermine those possibilities can then receive a penalty, reducing the need to list individual side effects by hand.

Preserving future possibilities creates a complication: an agent might interfere with other actors whose actions would make some future tasks impossible. The authors address this using a baseline policy representing a default course of action, such as doing nothing. They exclude future tasks that would already be unachievable under that baseline, so the agent is not rewarded for preventing every such loss.

The paper formally defines interference incentives and proves that its baseline-based approach avoids them in deterministic settings. Gridworld experiments also show avoidance of interference and better side-effect prevention than penalizing irreversible actions. These findings support evaluating consequences through future task availability while accounting for what would happen by default.
neurips-2020-avoiding-side-effects-by-co.tldr: An auxiliary reward protects future task possibilities, while a default-policy baseline prevents interference incentives in deterministic settings.

paragraphs: Molecular profiling produces multiple kinds of high-dimensional measurements about living systems. Understanding how these measurements relate across molecular classes can help reveal how signals pass through biological systems. BayReL addresses this integration problem by learning relationships between data types, rather than treating each collection of measurements as an isolated source of information.

The method uses a Bayesian representation-learning framework. Each data type forms a separate view, with previously known relationships among molecules represented as a graph within that view. BayReL uses these graphs to learn hidden representations specific to each view, together with a graph connecting molecules across views. This connecting graph explicitly represents the cross-type interactions the method aims to infer.

Experiments on several real-world datasets report better identification of meaningful interactions than existing comparison methods. The contribution is therefore a way to combine prior knowledge within molecular classes with learned relationships between classes. The reported findings support this structured integration strategy for recovering useful interactions from multi-omics data.
neurips-2020-bayrel-bayesian-relational-.tldr: BayReL combines known relationships within molecular data types to learn meaningful interactions across them.

paragraphs: COPT introduces a distance between graphs that also supports learning graph representations without supervision. The aim is to capture information useful for both comparing graphs and constructing graph sketches. Its distance is defined through an optimization problem, making the representation depend on how two graphs can be related through coordinated mappings.

The method jointly computes two optimal transport plans. One relates vertices in the two graphs; the other relates probability distributions of graph signals. Optimizing these plans together coordinates the vertex-level correspondence with the comparison of signal distributions. This paired construction is the central mechanism behind the proposed graph distance.

The authors prove that COPT preserves important information about overall graph structure, including spectral information. They also analyze its relationship to earlier work. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show better graph classification performance than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support COPT as a general-purpose representation approach that retains global structure relevant to downstream graph analysis.
neurips-2020-copt-coordinated-optimal-tr.tldr: COPT jointly transports vertices and graph-signal distributions to compare graphs while preserving important global structure.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers learning from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Methods that make the domains' representations look alike can struggle when class frequencies differ. This paper addresses that mismatch through generalized label shift: the assumption that a representation exists whose distribution is the same across domains when conditioned on the class label.

This distinction allows overall class proportions to change while requiring alignment within each class. Under the assumption, the authors establish transfer-performance guarantees for any classifier. They also derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the assumption to hold, using estimates of relative class weights and appropriate sample reweighting.

The weight-estimation procedure can be incorporated into existing methods that learn domain-invariant representations with little added computation. The authors modify JAN, DANN, and CDAN and evaluate them on standard and artificial adaptation tasks. The modified versions outperform their originals, with especially large gains when label distributions differ substantially. These results support explicitly accounting for class proportions during representation alignment.
neurips-2020-domain-adaptation-with-cond.tldr: Class-conditioned alignment and estimated class reweighting improve domain adaptation when source and target label proportions differ.

paragraphs: Some training objectives require derivatives of derivatives, which can consume substantial computation and memory even with automatic differentiation. Score matching provides an example in generative modeling because its objective involves the trace of a Hessian. This paper seeks a less expensive way to handle those derivative-dependent quantities during learning.

The authors rewrite score matching and related objectives using directional derivatives. They then introduce a general finite-difference strategy for approximating directional derivatives of any order. The approximation uses function evaluations that can run in parallel, without computing gradients for the derivative approximation itself. This reformulation reduces the computational burden and is also reported to improve numerical stability.

The paper gives two concrete versions by converting score-matching variants into finite-difference objectives. Empirical results show outcomes comparable to the corresponding gradient-based approaches with substantially greater computational efficiency. The significance is that an expensive mathematical ingredient can be approximated through simpler evaluations while preserving comparable generative-modeling results in the reported experiments.
neurips-2020-efficient-learning-of-gener.tldr: Finite-difference reformulations make score-matching training substantially more efficient while producing comparable empirical results.

paragraphs: Planning in a large Markov decision process becomes difficult when computation grows with the number of possible states. This paper develops a planning method whose runtime instead depends on a smaller feature-based description. It uses linear value-function approximation to represent the quality of states without requiring a separate value for every state.

The method assumes that the optimal value function can be approximated accurately and that a small collection of core states has features spanning those of the other states. These requirements concern the optimal value function and the coverage provided by core features. They do not require policies, or value functions belonging to non-optimal policies, to have suitable representations.

With access to a simulator for the decision process, the algorithm produces nearly optimal actions for any state. Its computation scales polynomially with the numbers of features, core states, and actions, and with the effective horizon. The result shows that efficient planning can be possible under these weaker approximation requirements without runtime scaling with the full state count.
neurips-2020-efficient-planning-in-large.tldr: A simulator-based planner finds nearly optimal actions with runtime independent of state count under weak linear approximation assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression under a distributional fairness requirement: predicted values should have the same distribution across groups defined by a sensitive feature. This extends demographic parity from classification to numerical predictions. The goal is to learn an accurate predictor while satisfying this specific constraint on how its outputs vary between groups.

The authors analyze a discretized proxy of the problem and derive an explicit form for its optimal fair predictor. That expression leads to a two-stage procedure. First, labeled data are used to estimate an ordinary regression function without the fairness constraint. A separate unlabeled dataset then supports recalibration of its outputs, using an efficient smooth optimization procedure.

The theoretical analysis gives convergence rates toward the optimal fair predictor for both predictive risk and the fairness constraint. Numerical experiments show that the method is often better than, or competitive with, leading alternatives. The approach matters because it turns the fairness requirement into a recalibration step backed by statistical guarantees, while retaining a conventional regression-estimation stage.
neurips-2020-fair-regression-via-plug-in.tldr: A two-stage regression method uses unlabeled-data recalibration to pursue demographic parity with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper examines which unbalanced optimal transport problems admit fast algorithms. Its central finding is that computational difficulty depends strongly on the distance structure used by the problem. It combines lower bounds for Euclidean distances with an exact algorithm for tree distances, separating settings where substantial speedups face a theoretical barrier from one where they are achievable.

For the Kantorovich–Rubinstein distance and optimal partial transport in Euclidean space, the authors rule out strongly subquadratic computation under the strong exponential time hypothesis. This is a conditional computational lower bound: it depends on that hypothesis. It identifies a barrier to improving runtime by a fixed polynomial factor over quadratic scaling.

On a tree metric, the authors solve a more general unbalanced transport problem exactly in quasi-linear time. They report processing a tree containing one million nodes in under one second. The combination of theory and implementation shows why tree structure can make very large transport computations practical while clarifying the difficulty of corresponding Euclidean problems.
neurips-2020-fast-unbalanced-optimal-tra.tldr: Unbalanced transport has conditional Euclidean runtime barriers, but a tree metric enables exact quasi-linear computation at million-node scale.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework linking neural-network optimization to generalization. The motivation is that common optimization analyses use infinite-width limits to establish global convergence, making finite-width networks harder to address directly. The authors seek a framework that can analyze both narrow and wide networks within the same mathematical treatment.

They formulate parameter training as estimation of a transportation map and analyze it through infinite-dimensional Langevin dynamics. Within this formulation, they establish global convergence. The infinite-dimensional dynamics provide the analytical machinery while the framework accommodates networks of different widths, avoiding a dependence on treating network width itself as infinite.

The analysis also bounds the generalization gap and excess risk of the solution produced by the dynamics. The excess-risk bound attains a fast learning rate. More specifically, the authors show exponential convergence for a classification problem and a minimax-optimal rate for a regression problem. These results connect successful optimization with statistical performance in the problems analyzed, extending the framework beyond convergence alone.
neurips-2020-generalization-bound-of-glo.tldr: A transportation-map formulation analyzes global convergence and generalization for narrow and wide networks through infinite-dimensional Langevin dynamics.

paragraphs: GRAPE addresses two related problems with incomplete data: estimating missing feature values and predicting labels from partially observed examples. Existing approaches often handle these separately, with imputation methods relying on strong prior assumptions and label-prediction methods using heuristics or facing scaling difficulties. The paper proposes a shared graph-based framework for both tasks.

It represents observations and features as two different kinds of nodes in a bipartite graph. An observed feature value becomes an edge connecting its observation to its feature. Under this representation, filling in a missing value becomes an edge-level prediction problem, while predicting an observation's label becomes a node-level prediction problem. Graph neural networks solve both types of prediction.

Across nine benchmark datasets, the authors report 20% lower mean absolute error for imputation and 10% lower error for label prediction compared with existing state-of-the-art methods. These results support organizing incomplete data around relationships between observations and features. The representation supplies a common learning structure for reconstructing missing entries and making downstream predictions.
neurips-2020-handling-missing-data-with-.tldr: GRAPE turns incomplete data into a bipartite graph so graph neural networks can predict both missing values and labels.

paragraphs: One-class learning builds a model from data belonging to a single class. The paper observes that neural approaches commonly use autoencoders or adversarial training to learn a hidden representation of that class. HRN instead centers its design on how the learning objective treats the available features, aiming to avoid a model that favors only some of them.

Its main component is holistic regularization, called H-regularization. This is designed to make the system consider the data as a whole rather than develop feature-specific bias. The authors combine it with a proposed instance-level normalization based on the 2-norm. Together, these two components form the HRN method, making regularization and normalization central to its approach.

The evaluation covers both benchmark image-classification datasets and traditional anomaly-detection datasets. The authors report that HRN substantially outperforms the deep and non-deep state-of-the-art methods compared in these experiments. The findings support this combination as an effective approach to one-class learning across the evaluated data settings.
neurips-2020-hrn-a-holistic-approach-to-.tldr: HRN combines holistic regularization with instance-level normalization to improve one-class learning on image and anomaly-detection benchmarks.

paragraphs: Automatic augmentation search needs to judge many candidate policies for transforming training data. Fully training and validating a model for each candidate is expensive, especially when evaluation occurs thousands of times. Faster substitutes can make policy judgments less reliable. This paper targets that evaluation bottleneck rather than treating speed and reliability as an unavoidable exchange.

The authors study the dynamics of training with augmented data and use the findings to construct a proxy task based on Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing. This proxy provides a faster way to assess candidate policies. Their analysis reports advantages in both effectiveness and efficiency, and the discovered policies outperform those found by existing automatic augmentation search methods.

On CIFAR-10, the reported top-1 error is 1.24%, described in the paper as the best single-model result without additional training data at that time. On ImageNet, ResNet-50 reaches 20.36% top-1 error, an absolute reduction of 3.34 percentage points over the baseline augmentation. These outcomes connect improved policy evaluation to stronger final models.
neurips-2020-improving-auto-augment-via-.tldr: Augmentation-Wise Weight Sharing speeds up augmentation-policy evaluation while finding policies that improve reported classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Iterative Deep Graph Learning jointly learns a graph's structure and representations of its nodes. Its guiding idea is reciprocal improvement: more useful node representations can reveal better connections, and better connections can support more useful representations. This makes the graph itself part of the learning process for the downstream prediction task.

The method repeatedly updates structure and embeddings, stopping dynamically when the learned structure is sufficiently close to the graph optimized for the task. It treats graph construction as learning a similarity metric and uses adaptive regularization to control the resulting graph's quality. An additional version uses anchor-based approximation to reduce both time and memory requirements without compromising reported performance.

Experiments across nine benchmarks show that the models consistently match or outperform state-of-the-art comparison methods. The paper also reports that the approach can be more robust to adversarial graphs and can handle both transductive and inductive learning. These findings support refining connectivity alongside representations rather than taking graph structure as a fixed input throughout training.
neurips-2020-iterative-deep-graph-learni.tldr: Iteratively refining graph structure and node embeddings improves prediction, with a scalable approximation and reported robustness benefits.

paragraphs: Many latent-variable models describe observed data using a low-rank matrix. This structure appears in applications including community detection, collaborative filtering, genomics, and language processing. The paper asks how many samples are needed to recover such matrices efficiently, establishing bounds in several common latent-variable settings where that requirement had remained unresolved.

For a k-by-k matrix of rank r, the authors show that attaining normalized L1 error ε requires at least order kr/ε² samples. Their algorithm uses order (kr/ε²) log²(r/ε) samples. Thus, its sample requirement matches the lower bound apart from a logarithmic factor, scaling linearly with the matrix dimension and nearly linearly with rank.

The algorithm runs in polynomial time and improves on existing spectral techniques. Its proofs also establish new results about how rapidly the spectral distance between model and observation matrices converges. Together, these contributions quantify the sample scale needed for learning in the analyzed settings and provide an efficient procedure that comes close to that statistical requirement.
neurips-2020-linear-sample-learning-of-l.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm learns low-rank matrices with sample requirements matching established lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Neurons or filters with strongly correlated weights can weaken a network's ability to generalize. This paper proposes a regularizer that encourages diversity among those weights. It focuses on their directions: after normalization, weight vectors lie on a hypersphere, where their angular separation provides a way to describe how similarly they are oriented.

The method maximizes the smallest pairwise angles between normalized vectors. Improving this minimum separation encourages the vectors to spread more uniformly over the sphere. The design is inspired by the Tammes problem and becomes part of ordinary training by adding a regularization term to the loss. The authors report that the additional computational cost is negligible.

Experiments show improvements in generalization across several modern models, with substantial performance gains on CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet. Face-verification experiments also support its effectiveness for learning features. These results suggest that directly discouraging closely aligned weight directions can be a useful training regularizer, with a simple integration mechanism and little reported computational overhead.
neurips-2020-mma-regularization-decorrel.tldr: MMA regularization spreads normalized weight directions apart to improve neural-network generalization with negligible reported overhead.

paragraphs: Combining brain measurements across subjects is difficult because anatomy, functional organization, and stimulus responses vary between individuals. Naturalistic experiments such as movie watching add complexity because they do not isolate clearly defined cognitive operations. This paper develops MultiView ICA to identify shared sources while allowing subjects to express those sources through different linear combinations.

Each subject's data are modeled as a mixture of shared independent sources plus noise. The model has a closed-form likelihood, unlike most group-ICA procedures discussed by the authors. An alternating quasi-Newton method maximizes that likelihood and is reported to be robust and fast to converge, providing a practical estimation procedure for the shared-source model.

On fMRI data, the method improves sensitivity to common sources and recovers sources with less variability across sessions than comparison methods. On MEG phantom data, it improves source localization. Applied to 200 Cam-CAN participants, it reveals a clear sequence of evoked activity in both sensor and source space, demonstrating utility across the reported neuroimaging settings.
neurips-2020-modeling-shared-responses-i.tldr: MultiView ICA models subjects as different mixtures of shared sources, improving reported source recovery and stability in neuroimaging.

paragraphs: Inferring another agent's goal is harder when its actions include mistakes, failure, or backtracking. This paper develops an architecture that updates goal estimates as actions arrive, including when behavior is non-optimal. It models agents as planners with limited reasoning resources who alternate between searching for plans and executing actions, replanning along the way.

The planning models are expressed as probabilistic programs, allowing Bayesian inference over both goals and internal planning processes. The authors introduce Sequential Inverse Plan Search, or SIPS, to carry out this inference. This sequential Monte Carlo algorithm exploits the replanning assumption by incrementally extending inferred plans as new actions are observed, limiting the computation needed for updates.

Experiments show more accurate goal inference than Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning baselines for both optimal and non-optimal trajectories, including failure and backtracking. The architecture also generalizes across domains with compositional structure and sparse rewards. These findings support modeling imperfect planning explicitly when interpreting behavior, so unsuccessful actions can still provide evidence about what an agent intends.
neurips-2020-online-bayesian-goal-infere.tldr: SIPS infers goals online by modeling limited planning and replanning, allowing failures and backtracking to remain informative.

paragraphs: Community detection groups entities using their observed pairwise interactions. In many applications, an entity can belong to several communities, so forcing every node into a single group is restrictive. This paper studies overlapping communities in weighted graphs, where interactions carry weights and community membership need not be exclusive.

A common assumption in overlapping-community methods is that every community contains at least one pure node: a node belonging only to that community. Such exclusive members may be absent in practice. The authors provide a method with theoretical guarantees without explicitly imposing this pure-node assumption, addressing a structural restriction that can make other approaches less suitable.

Their method is based on convex optimization, bringing established theoretical properties of that optimization framework to the community-detection problem. The authors also demonstrate successful behavior on artificial and real-world datasets. The contribution combines a provable approach with empirical evidence while allowing communities to overlap without explicitly requiring an exclusive representative for each one.
neurips-2020-provable-overlapping-commun.tldr: A convex optimization method detects overlapping communities in weighted graphs without explicitly assuming each community has an exclusive member.

paragraphs: Metric learning adapts the notion of distance used for classification and similarity search. This paper asks whether learned distances remain reliable under small adversarial changes to their inputs. The authors show that methods emphasizing accuracy on unperturbed data can produce metrics that are less robust than ordinary Euclidean distance.

They propose an algorithm that learns a Mahalanobis distance with robustness as an explicit goal. The resulting model has certifiable robustness, providing a guarantee rather than relying only on observed behavior under selected attacks. This changes the learning objective from improving clean performance alone to constructing a distance that also supports protection against adversarial perturbations.

Experiments report improvements in both certified robust error and empirical error under adversarial attacks. The method also avoids sacrificing clean-data error relative to previous metric-learning methods in the reported comparisons. These findings show that the robustness weaknesses identified in conventional metric learning can be addressed while retaining clean performance, rather than assuming that a learned distance is automatically safer or more reliable.
neurips-2020-provably-robust-metric-lear.tldr: A certifiably robust metric-learning algorithm improves adversarial performance without sacrificing clean performance in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Labels have two competing effects when some classes are much more common than others. They provide useful supervision, but majority classes can disproportionately shape the classifier's decision boundary. This paper investigates both effects, asking how labels should be used when their distribution is heavily imbalanced rather than assuming more direct supervision is always preferable.

The authors develop two complementary strategies. In a semi-supervised setting, existing labels can be combined with additional unlabeled data to reduce label bias and improve the final classifier. In a self-supervised setting, classifiers first learn through pretraining without class-label supervision. The paper reports that these pretrained classifiers consistently outperform their corresponding baselines in its evaluations.

The strategies receive both theoretical and empirical support, with extensive experiments on large-scale imbalanced datasets outperforming previous state-of-the-art approaches. The findings show that imbalanced labels remain valuable, but their value depends on how they enter learning. Additional unlabeled data and self-supervised pretraining offer different ways to reduce the influence of class imbalance while retaining useful supervision.
neurips-2020-rethinking-the-value-of-lab.tldr: Semi-supervised learning and self-supervised pretraining improve imbalanced classification by changing how skewed labels influence learning.

paragraphs: A network's Lipschitz constant describes how strongly its output can change relative to changes in its input. Estimating this quantity matters for applications including robustness certification and Wasserstein generative adversarial networks. This paper develops an optimization framework for estimating both global and local Lipschitz constants of multilayer ReLU networks.

The approach introduces a hierarchy of semidefinite programs. Its key construction combines a polynomial lifting of ReLU derivatives with a weak generalization of Putinar's positivity certificate. This translates the derivative-based estimation problem into a form that the proposed optimization hierarchy can address. The authors also suggest that the construction could extend to other nearly sparse polynomial optimization problems in machine learning.

Empirical comparisons reveal a trade-off relative to a state-of-the-art linear programming approach. In some cases, the proposed method obtains better bounds while taking less time. The stated contribution is therefore an additional way to balance bound quality and computation, with demonstrated improvements in particular cases rather than a claim of uniform superiority.
neurips-2020-semialgebraic-optimization-.tldr: A semidefinite programming hierarchy estimates ReLU-network Lipschitz constants, sometimes producing better bounds faster than a linear programming approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a high-dimensional signal from noisy nonlinear measurements when the signal lies in the range of a generative model. The model maps bounded k-dimensional inputs into n-dimensional signals and is L-Lipschitz continuous. This structure supplies a low-dimensional description of the signals eligible for recovery.

Using a generalized Lasso approach, the authors analyze sub-Gaussian measurement models and allow adversarial corruption. Under independent, identically distributed Gaussian measurements, they establish a non-uniform guarantee requiring roughly order (k/ε²) log L samples for Euclidean error ε. The recovery scheme is also robust to adversarial noise. The bound ties the sample requirement to the generator's input dimension and regularity.

The authors apply the result to neural-network generators and discuss extensions to other models and measurements that are not independent and identically distributed. A uniform recovery guarantee is also available under an additional local embedding property, which they show holds for 1-bit and censored Tobit models. The stronger guarantee therefore retains a specific additional assumption.
neurips-2020-the-generalized-lasso-with-.tldr: Generalized Lasso recovers signals described by Lipschitz generators from nonlinear measurements, with conditional sample and robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers a predictor from labeled source data to a target domain without labels. Most methods emphasize target accuracy, but a useful prediction also needs a meaningful confidence estimate. This paper examines calibration in that setting, where domain differences and missing target labels jointly make predictive uncertainty difficult to assess.

The authors identify a tension: adaptation models can improve accuracy while producing less well-calibrated probabilities. They propose Transferable Calibration, or TransCal, to address that problem through a unified optimization framework with lower bias and variance. The framework is described as hyperparameter-free, and its purpose is to improve calibration after a domain-adaptation model has been learned.

As a general post-hoc method, TransCal can recalibrate existing adaptation approaches. The paper supports its effectiveness with both theory and experiments. Its contribution is to treat confidence quality as a distinct requirement of successful transfer, showing that accuracy gains alone do not establish that a model's probabilities are dependable in the new domain.
neurips-2020-transferable-calibration-wi.tldr: TransCal recalibrates domain-adaptation models through a hyperparameter-free framework designed to reduce calibration bias and variance.

paragraphs: Deep functional-map methods address shape matching using a variety of supervision levels, loss functions, and regularization choices. This diversity leaves an important design question: which components are actually needed for strong results? The paper investigates the essential ingredients of these pipelines and whether a common design can account for different existing approaches.

The authors empirically identify minimum components that obtain state-of-the-art results with different losses, including supervised and unsupervised ones. This is an experimental finding about effective pipeline design. It helps connect results across training setups by examining the components supporting them, rather than considering every combination of loss and supervision as an unrelated method.

Building on that investigation, the paper introduces a weakly supervised framework for both matching complete shapes to complete shapes and matching partial shapes to complete ones. It achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets, including improvements over fully supervised methods. These findings show that the proposed pipeline can deliver strong matching performance without requiring the highest level of supervision used by its competitors.
neurips-2020-weakly-supervised-deep-func.tldr: An empirical study of essential functional-map components leads to a weakly supervised shape matcher that outperforms fully supervised methods on benchmarks.
